item.title: US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck05rrj3jeylo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship - Published The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration using a controversial federal database that relies on citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens. Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls. In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans. But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibited broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, thus limiting any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms. States can still check the citizenship of individual voters. The three liberal-leaning justices on the Supreme Court dissented from the majority decision. One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters. "The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote. The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (Save), allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls. The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits. But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls. In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system showed that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote". A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday. The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information. The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary. The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task". Voting rights groups called the ruling "profoundly disappointing". "It puts millions of Americans at risk of being unlawfully targeted by the administration's unreliable voter purge database weeks before the midterm elections," the League of Women Voters, the lead plaintiff in the case, said in a statement. "We will be doing everything in our power to protect Americans' voting and privacy rights by ensuring that the district court decision stands." Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship. Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes. For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports. Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas. Some states, like Georgia, have worked with the government on the Save programme. Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, a Republican, has touted his office's work with the programme and his recommendations to improve the system. Raffensperger told the BBC that his office thoroughly vetted the government-provided data to determine whether flagged individuals were non-citizens, even interviewsing some of the voters in question to ensure accuracy. "There's always guardrails in place, to make sure that we never denied the right to vote," Raffensperger said. Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to rein in mail-in ballots. In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters. The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls. Additional reporting by Kayla Epstein

item.title: Two arrested after people seen mysteriously emerging from various New York City sewers
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwddvv44091vo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Two arrested after people seen mysteriously emerging from various New York City sewers - Published New York officials have arrested two of three men who they said were seen emerging from a manhole to exit the city's underground sewer system on Wednesday. The New York Police Department (NYPD) arrested 26-year-old Kevin Rodriguez and 25-year-old Samuel Reveron on charges of conspiracy and trespassing. Three men were seen exiting a manhole near the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reportedly expected to stay for the United Nations General Assembly. The NYPD said in a statement to the BBC that it had seen a number of incidents involving people going into the sewer system to look for valuables and scrap metal after a storm. "This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the UN General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said. Rodriguez and Reveron, both from the borough of Queens, were arrested on Thursday. They allegedly fled the scene after climbing out of the manhole when officers were called around 04:30 EST (08:30 GMT) on Wednesday, police said. During a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody, according to court records. The arrests follow a string of incidents in which people were seen emerging from pavement manholes in different parts of the city in recent months. In August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning. The same month, the NYPD said it was investigating three people wearing overalls and headlamps seen climbing out of a manhole near Penn Station. In May, a group of people were captured on surveillance footage shifting a manhole cover and climbing down into the sewer in South Brooklyn. Going into the New York sewer system is both illegal and dangerous, officials have said, cautioning that there was a risk of toxic gases and flooding in a confined space. "For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole or outfall," the city's Department of Environmental Protection previously told the BBC. This year, a woman died after she opened her car door and accidentally fell into an open manhole in Midtown Manhattan.

item.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5ydvww0erdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever - Published The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries. The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history. They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it. But now, nearly all the snow is gone. A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks. But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two. Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime. "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow". She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas. Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool. But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it. Proof of a warming planet The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall. El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace. The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says. A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds. The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape". A spiritual anchor At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations. The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow". "Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity." According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live. Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts. "How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed." For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event. The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape. Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys. Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment. "Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people." As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left. Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains. From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts." Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change. "When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains. Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed. "I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation." Related topics - Published11 June - Published17 September

item.title: What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjn5ddzekwnro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What is kratom, the 'gas station heroin' alarming officials in the US? - Published Jeffrey Deaver, a 58-year-old retired timber cutter in the state of Washington, has taken kratom for four years to help with severe chronic hip and knee pain. He discovered the herbal product when he couldn't find relief from doctors and while waiting for surgeries. Scared at first, he "started small", but then took more until his pain went away. "It was like a miracle," Deaver said. "I could sleep. I could function. "I just don't know what I'd do without it." Kratom - a herb with opioid-like effects - has grown in popularity in the US over the last decade, and is typically purchased over the counter and consumed in pill or liquid form. This week, investigators found packaged kratom in the possession of two deceased University of Mississippi students. Although their deaths were not attributed to kratom, officials are now issuing warnings about its consumption. For years, anti-kratom advocates have pushed for bans, and in some countries, like the UK, it's illegal. But Kratom is not regulated by the US Food and Drug Administration and is legal in some states, including Mississippi. Here's what we know about it: What is kratom? Kratom is a tree that is native to Southeast Asia in countries like Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. It's been used for centuries for its stimulant properties, grounded and consumed similar to tea. As its popularity spread around the globe, it entered the US market as a supplement around 2016. "That's really where the problems began," said Dr Shane Speights, dean of the New York Institute of Technology College of Osteopathic Medicine at Arkansas State University. In the US kratom is mostly sold in highly concentrated forms either via pill, powder or liquid, Speights said. It's also widely available - found everywhere from convenience stores and petrol stations to vape shops. Also, because of the supplement classification, kratom products are not federally regulated. "There's no way to know exactly what you're getting," Speight said. "You could go and create something in your basement, market it as a supplement, and nobody's really going to check and see what's in it." What is kratom used for? Kratom is often marketed as a safe, natural herbal supplement that helps with pain management, anxiety and depression. In lower doses, its stimulant properties create a "caffeine-kind of buzz", Speights explained. Because of its opioid-like effects, it has also been used with the goal of curbing addictions to actual opioids like fentanyl. Those properties stem from the way the plant's compounds - like 7-Hydroxymitragynine - activate various hormones, including dopamine. What are the effects and how dangerous is it? "It's almost like taking a narcotic," Speights said. "At higher doses, it can create more euphoria and give you more of a general high." Hallucinations are possible, too. The higher doses also pose greater risk for adverse side effects. That includes central nervous system (CNS) depression - which is "where the deaths come in," Speights said. CNS can result in cardiovascular collapse and loss of breathing. Withdrawal symptoms and addiction are also risks, said Jana Wu, director of clinical integration at the addiction treatment centre Mountainside. "It affects marriages, relationships," she said. "I've seen people lose jobs, spend thousands of dollars a month on it." Because it's easy to develop a high tolerance to the herb, users may need to take an increasing amount to achieve the same effect over time. "I've worked with people that were taking like up to 20 pills a day," Wu said. Experts told the BBC that the biggest dangers come from the fact that kratom is not federally regulated. "Is there a safe dose?" Speights said. "My answer is going to be no because - I'm going to go back to this - we don't know what's in it." Is kratom legal? Kratom is banned in 11 states: Alabama, Arkansas, Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Massachusetts, North Dakota, Tennessee, Vermont and Wisconsin. Massachusetts was the last state to make it illegal, issuing a temporary emergency order in August. Ten years earlier, the US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) had moved to classify kratom as a Schedule 1, the most dangerous level for drugs, calling it "an imminent hazard to public safety". But the effort failed a few months later, after the justice department said it received "numerous comments from members of the public challenging" the attempt. That leaves states to take action, like Arizona, which recently sued a company selling kratom beverage products. Groups opposed to kratom want states to do more, saying "gas-station drugs are poisoning our communities". Pro-kratom groups like the American Kratom Association are pushing for bans against synthetics "posing as natural kratom". Internationally, kratom is banned in the UK. In Europe, the laws vary by country. In Malaysia, where the kratom tree is native, consumption and sale are banned under the Poisons Act of 1952.

item.title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2zlqeje9zo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare - Published A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance. Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis. But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years. It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities. Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again. A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more. A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story. A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time. Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity. And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered. That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results. In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap). But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch. It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue. Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people. Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU. Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag. "I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way." Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy. He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition. And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success. This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year. But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue. Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector. It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy. And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration. While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD). Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence. Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania. Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered. The AfD has survived numerous scandals in recent years to now top the polls nationwide, at around 28%. It carries the swagger of a party making the political weather. It has capitalised on a nostalgia for the past alongside an anxiety in the present as it consolidates its strongholds in the former communist east. An AfD placard I saw in Berlin read "Berlin braucht Ordnung" (Berlin needs order). It is the as yet untested promise that this party can bring back a lost sense of stability. But in Germany's capital it was in fact Die Linke (the Left) that topped the polls last Sunday in a further blow to the country's traditional "big tent" parties. The victory has put fresh scrutiny on Die Linke, as it faces allegations of antisemitism. The party leadership has insisted it is committed to protecting Jewish life. This round of regional elections has encapsulated the country's fault lines: the eroding support for Germany's political centre, and a polarising debate on the AfD. Rarely in post-war Germany has a set of local polls generated so much upheaval at home and interest abroad.

item.title: How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6d94wywx0ypo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray? - Published Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army. Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict. There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted. This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago. Why has fighting broken out now? It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray. The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions. This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting. This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation. The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray. Who are the TPLF? For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government. It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades. At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population. When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence. Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century. The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine. An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022. Why has the peace deal faltered? There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray. The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army. Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991. When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa. The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum. For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms. The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy. But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy. This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions. Who is backing the TPLF? A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies. Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army. Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power. So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside. TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated. Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests. What is the government's position? As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country. It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies. During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out. Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports. Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force. What do we know about the bombing in Tigray? Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces. The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify. Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war. This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces. The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks. What is being done to stop the fighting? The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks. It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently. The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict. The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume. The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated. Could the fighting spread? Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia. The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia. The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily. There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government. The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters. The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.
